claims.text: Increasing a selected dopant concentration from 0 to about 10 at.% amplifies lattice distortion in an HEA coating.
Increasing the dopant concentration stabilizes tribo-layers at the sliding interface.
Greater lattice distortion can contribute to improved wear resistance in HEAs.
Doping up to about 10 at.% measurably improves the sliding-wear performance of an HEA coating.
An equimolar HEA coating can be deposited by sputtering from an equimolar target.
A suitable dopant can enhance lattice strain while retaining single-phase stability over the proposed 0–10 at.% range.
Loads of 1–5 N and sliding speeds of 0.1–0.5 m/s are representative of typical industrial sliding conditions.
Dopant-induced lattice strain reduces dislocation mobility.
Dopant-induced lattice strain promotes formation of a stable surface tribo-layer.
Reduced dislocation mobility and a stable tribo-layer mitigate material removal.
Reduced dislocation mobility and a stable tribo-layer lower the steady-state friction coefficient.
Doped coatings will have lower wear rates than otherwise similar undoped or minimally doped coatings.
Doped coatings will have lower friction coefficients than otherwise similar undoped or minimally doped coatings.
Doped coatings will form more resilient tribofilms than the baseline coatings.
The beneficial effect should persist up to about 10 at.% dopant at room or slightly elevated temperature, provided a single-phase HEA structure is preserved.
Above about 10 at.% dopant, excessive phase segregation may degrade mechanical properties.
Above about 10 at.% dopant, phase segregation may disrupt tribofilm formation and limit the beneficial wear effect.
